title: Properties of Logarithms
presenterNotes: Emphasize the connection between exponent rules and log properties. Students often memorize the log rules but forget they come from exponents.
When expanding and condensing, stress the order: for expanding, quotient first, then product, then power. For condensing, reverse: power, product, quotient.
The Change-of-Base formula is a practical tool. Have students practice with both common and natural logs to see they get the same result.
The decibel example is a great real-world application. Walk through the cancellation carefully so students see why the increase is constant.
In the Blueprint block, encourage students to factor the argument into numbers whose logs they know. This is a key strategy for log evaluation problems.

discoveryHook.scenario: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, division into subtraction, and powers into multiplication—massively simplifying complex calculations. This was the secret behind slide rules and early science!

confusionCorner.title: Log of Sum Is Not Sum of Logs
confusionCorner.body: The Product Property works for multiplication inside the log. For addition, $\log_b(m+n)$ cannot be simplified. [[imp:$\log_b(m+n) \neq \log_b m + \log_b n$]]

explanation: Logarithms have three fundamental properties that mirror exponent rules.
[[kw:Product Property]]: $\log_b (mn) = \log_b m + \log_b n$. The log of a product is the sum of the logs.
[[kw:Quotient Property]]: $\log_b \left( \frac{m}{n} \right) = \log_b m - \log_b n$. The log of a quotient is the difference of the logs.
[[kw:Power Property]]: $\log_b (m^n) = n \log_b m$. The log of a power is the exponent times the log of the base.
These properties are valid for any positive base $b \neq 1$ and positive arguments $m, n$.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \log_b(mn) = \log_b m + \log_b n $$ $$ \log_b\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \log_b m - \log_b n $$ $$ \log_b(m^n) = n \log_b m $$

legend.meaning: write as sum/difference of simpler logs

explanation: [[kw:Expanding]] a logarithmic expression means writing it as a sum, difference, or product of simpler logarithms.
Use the properties in order: Quotient Property first (if a fraction), then Product Property, then Power Property.
[[kw:Condensing]] means combining multiple logarithmic terms into a single logarithm.
Condense in reverse order: Power Property first (move coefficients to exponents), then Product Property, then Quotient Property.

examples.prompt: Use Change-of-Base to find $\log_2 10$. Round to two decimal places.

explanation: The [[kw:Change-of-Base Formula]] allows you to rewrite a logarithm in terms of logs with a different base: $$ \log_c a = \frac{\log_b a}{\log_b c} $$
Common choices for the new base $b$ are 10 (common log) and $e$ (natural log).
Using common logs: $\log_c a = \frac{\log a}{\log c}$.
Using natural logs: $\log_c a = \frac{\ln a}{\ln c}$.
This is especially useful for evaluating logs with bases other than 10 or $e$ on a calculator.

Introduce the formula: $\log_c a = \frac{\log a}{\log c}$ or $\frac{\ln a}{\ln c}$.

confusionCorner.body: The original argument goes on top, the original base goes on the bottom. [[imp:$\log_c a = \frac{\log a}{\log c}$, not $\frac{\log c}{\log a}$.]] A common mistake is flipping the fraction.

What property of logs allows you to write $\log 2I - \log I = \log 2$?
hints: Subtraction of logs becomes division inside.

explanation: Many real‑life formulas use logarithms, such as sound loudness $L(I) = 10\log\frac{I}{I_0}$ (decibels).
Log properties allow us to simplify changes. If intensity doubles, the increase is $L(2I) - L(I) = 10(\log 2 + \log\frac{I}{I_0} - \log\frac{I}{I_0}) = 10\log 2$.
Notice that the $\log\frac{I}{I_0}$ terms cancel, leaving a constant increase that does not depend on the original intensity.
This shows the power of log properties: they turn multiplicative changes (doubling) into additive changes ($+10\log 2$ dB).

confusionCorner.title: Decibel Scale Is Logarithmic
confusionCorner.body: An increase of 10 dB means 10 times the intensity. An increase of 20 dB means 100 times the intensity. The scale is not linear; each 10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10. [[imp:Decibels measure ratios on a log scale.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: When a sound's intensity doubles, the decibel increase is $10\log 2 \approx 3$ dB—a barely noticeable change. This uses the Quotient and Product Properties to simplify a real-world logarithmic expression.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid — Using Log Properties to Solve Problems

discoveryHook.scenario: With log properties and the Blueprint, you can evaluate unfamiliar logarithms using known values—just like detectives piecing together clues. Break the argument into factors, use properties, and solve step by step.

rows.1: Identify target; factor argument using known values.
Apply Product/Quotient/Power Properties; substitute known values.

visuals.title: Blueprint for Evaluating Logs with Properties

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the target logarithm and the given logarithmic values. Look for ways to rewrite the argument as a product, quotient, or power of numbers whose logs are known.
[[imp:Solve]]: Apply the appropriate properties (Product, Quotient, Power) to break the target into known pieces. If needed, use Change-of-Base to evaluate with a calculator.
[[imp:Conclude]]: Substitute the known values and simplify. State the final approximate or exact value.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Mix Up Bases
confusionCorner.body: The Product, Quotient, and Power Properties only work when all logarithms have the [[imp:same base]]. You cannot combine $\log_2 x + \log_3 y$ using these properties without first converting to a common base.
